gap: No result ChatGPT got states what each converter costs per watt of real 220→110 V conversion. The two products ChatGPT showed (TESSAN 250 W, Ceptics 200 W) work out to $0.18–0.20 per W and cover only 10–12.5% of the 2,000 W that VoltWander says a US hair dryer needs. Ceptics' pure-sine VC-S2000, which also has universal plugs, converts 2,000 W at $0.065 per W.
standout_why: VoltWander's FAQ gives the 2,000 W+ hair-dryer figure, which is the 2,000 W yardstick used here, but it names no products, prices or cost per watt. MOMAX's guide says to check the continuous rating but gives no headroom rule, no products and no prices. The AAA 'Power Abroad' page and the Digital Camera World Ceptics review would not load past their titles, so I could not check them. ChatGPT's answer shows two 200–250 W units at $41.97 and $59.99. It does not work out how much wattage each one covers, and it does not warn that the '200 W' outlet on some combo units passes 220 V straight through without converting it.
decides: The answer to 'is there one?' is yes, but the pick depends on the device. For phones and small electronics, the TESSAN TC03 ($43.99, 250 W) and Ceptics PU-200C ($34.99, 200 W) cost about the same per watt (~$0.175/W). For a US hair dryer, neither 200–250 W unit is enough (250 ÷ 2,000 = 12.5%). The cheap 'dual' units, TESSAN's 4-USB model ($45.99) and Ceptics LX-C2000/LX2-M2000 ($49.99), get to 2,000 W only on a heating-appliance outlet. Ceptics says its LX-C2000 2,000 W outlet does not work with dryers that have circuit boards (Dyson, Shark FlexStyle). Only the Ceptics VC-S2000 ($129.99) converts 2,000 W pure sine wave on both outlets, and Ceptics allows a Dyson on it if nothing else is plugged in. That makes it the pick for 'one box for everything,' and the cheapest per watt among the universal-plug units.
